Item 9 — Example: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}] be a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and [MATH: [1; − 3]] What are the coordinates of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] relative to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},] where [MATH: \mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_2-\mathbf{b}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}_2 = 2\mathbf{b}_1 - 3\mathbf{b}_2?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given that

[MATH: {c_{1} = b_{2} − b_{1}; c_{2} = 2b_{1} − 3b_{2}.]

First, we express the [MATH: \mathbf{b}]'s in terms of [MATH: \mathbf{c}]'s. Multiplying the first equation by [MATH: 2] and adding the equations, we get

[MATH: 2\mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.]

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: \mathbf{c}_1 = \left( -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2 \right) - \mathbf{b}_1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_1 = -3\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.]

Since [MATH: [1; − 3]] we can write the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] in terms of the vectors [MATH: \mathbf c_1] and [MATH: \mathbf c_2,] as follows:

[MATH: x|= b_{1} − 3b_{2}; = (− 3c_{1} − c_{2}) − 3(− 2c_{1} − c_{2}); = − 3c_{1} − c_{2} + 6c_{1} + 3c_{2}; = 3c_{1} + 2c_{2}]

Therefore, [MATH: [3; 2]]
